Nationwide General Strike in Ecuador Disrupts Economic Activity, Major Firms Impacted

QUITO, June 12—A sweeping general strike brought economic activity to a near halt across Ecuador on Wednesday, with unions and civil society organizations demanding government action on wages and fuel prices, according to officials and industry groups.

The strike, which began early Wednesday morning, saw thousands of workers from transportation, construction, education, and healthcare sectors walk off the job, snarling traffic and shuttering businesses in Quito, Guayaquil, and other major cities. Airport access was limited in several regions, as bus and taxi drivers participated in the work stoppage, while ports operated at reduced capacity.

Among the companies affected is Holcim Ecuador SA, a key supplier to the construction sector. The company said in a statement that its cement shipments and plant operations had been “significantly disrupted” due to blocked highways and workforce shortages. “We are closely monitoring the situation and prioritizing the safety of our employees,” the statement read.

The Ecuadorian Chamber of Commerce estimated that Wednesday’s walkout could cost the economy up to $50 million in lost output if disruptions persist. “The current strike is having a widespread impact, especially on logistics and supply chains,” said Jaime Pérez, a spokesperson for the chamber. “Small businesses are particularly vulnerable to prolonged interruptions.”

Union leaders said the strike would continue until the government agrees to substantive negotiations. “We are united in our call for fair wages and affordable fuel,” said María Beltrán, a spokesperson for the National Workers’ Front. “The government must listen to the people.”

The Ministry of Labor reported that public services were operating at “minimum levels,” while police maintained a presence at key intersections and government buildings. Education officials confirmed that classes were suspended in most public schools nationwide.

Economists warned that a protracted shutdown could further strain Ecuador’s fragile recovery from last year’s recession. “Every day of stoppage compounds the challenges faced by businesses and households,” said analyst Diego Ordoñez.

Government officials had not announced any breakthrough by late afternoon, as negotiations remained stalled. Further updates were expected as the strike continued into the evening.
